lessonActivities.title: Who vs. Whom: The Subject/Object Test 🎯
lessonActivities.content:
Who = subject (does the action). Whom = object (receives the action). 🎯 Use the substitution test:

Test: Replace with he/she/they → use who. Replace with him/her/them → use whom.

PronounFunctionTestExample
whoSubjectHe/She/They + verbThe person who called → He called ✅
whomObjectVerb + him/her/themThe person whom I called → I called him ✅

Modern usage: In speech, 'who' often replaces 'whom' ✅ 'Who did you invite?' But in formal writing or after prepositions, use 'whom': ✅ 'To whom it may concern.'

Fun fact: 'Whom' is required after quantifiers: 'most of whom', 'several of whom' 🎯
examples: Subject: The woman who spoke was brilliant → She spoke ✅
Object: The woman whom we met was brilliant → We met her ✅
Preposition: The person to whom I spoke (formal) ✅
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Quick Test: Answer the question with 'him/her/them'? → use WHOM. 'He/she/they'? → use WHO.

lessonActivities.title: Which vs. That: Defining Clause Nuances 🚀
lessonActivities.content:
That and which both describe things—but usage depends on clause type and register.

American English Preference:

  • Defining clauses (essential info): Prefer that (no commas). The car that I bought is red.
  • Non-defining clauses (extra info): Use which (with commas). My car, which I bought last year, is red.
Clause TypePreferred PronounCommas?Example
Definingthat (or which)❌ NoThe book that I read
Non-definingwhich (never that)✅ YesThis book, which I read, is great
Formal Writingwhich for non-defining✅ YesThe data, which were collected...

Fun fact: British English is more flexible with 'which' in defining clauses, but American style guides strongly prefer 'that' for defining! 🌍
examples: Defining: The movie that/which we saw (both OK, 'that' more natural in speech)
Non-defining: My car, which is red (never 'that')
Formal: The methodology which was used (academic writing)
functions: Adapt to American vs. British style
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Memory trick: Defining = that (no commas) | Non-defining = which (commas). When in doubt, 'that' is safer for defining clauses.

lessonActivities.title: Prepositions + Pronouns: Formal Placement 🌟
lessonActivities.content:
In formal English, prepositions go before 'whom' or 'which'. In informal speech, they often go at the end.

Formal: The person to whom I spoke... ✅
Informal: The person (who) I spoke to... ✅

RegisterStructureExampleWhen to Use
Formal/Writtenpreposition + whom/whichThe house in which I liveAcademic, legal, professional
Informal/Spokenpronoun (optional) + ... + prepositionThe house (that) I live inConversation, casual writing
Avoidpreposition + who❌ to whoAlways incorrect

Key rule: After prepositions, never use 'who'—use 'whom' for people, 'which' for things.

Fun fact: 'Where' = 'in which', so you don't need an extra preposition! ✅ 'The city where I live' = 'The city in which I live' 🌍
examples: Formal: The colleague with whom I worked...
Informal: The colleague (who) I worked with...
Place shortcut: The office where I work (NOT 'in where')
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Never forget: After prepositions → WHOM (people) / WHICH (things). In speech → preposition at end is natural.

quizActivities.question: Who or whom? Substitution test:
quizActivities.explanation: 'Who' is subject pronoun. 'He called you' → subject → 'Who called you?'

quizActivities.question: Formal object pronoun:
quizActivities.explanation: Prepositions require 'whom' for people in formal English: 'to whom', 'with whom'.

quizActivities.question: Defining clause pronoun preference (American English):
quizActivities.hint: American style prefers 'that' in defining clauses
quizActivities.explanation: While both are grammatically correct, American English style guides recommend 'that' for defining clauses about things.

quizActivities.question: Non-defining clause rule:
quizActivities.sentence: My car, ____ is red, is fast.
quizActivities.explanation: 'That' cannot introduce non-defining clauses. Use 'which' with commas for extra information.

quizActivities.question: Quantifier + whom rule:
quizActivities.sentence: The participants, most of ____ completed the survey,
quizActivities.explanation: When a relative pronoun follows a quantifier ('most of', 'several of'), 'whom' is required for people in formal writing.

quizActivities.question: Formal preposition placement:
quizActivities.explanation: Academic and professional writing prefers 'in which' over 'where' for precision, though both are correct.

quizActivities.question: Identify register error:
quizActivities.sentence: The person to who I spoke. (the error: ____ )
quizActivities.explanation: 'To who' is grammatically incorrect. After prepositions, use 'whom' for people: 'to whom'.

quizActivities.question: Advanced: Best for academic abstract:
quizActivities.sentence: The framework, ____ was developed by Smith, ____ has been widely adopted,
quizActivities.explanation: Both clauses are non-defining (extra info about 'framework'), so 'which' is correct for both. Parallel structure enhances clarity in formal writing.
